default, or completely removed","articleBody":"You need to leave the metrics disabled by default and then at least ask users, first time they activate the editor, whether they would allow it to be enabled.\n\nI for one will not allow spyware to run on my box, hence I disable or remove such applications, but Atom doesn't provide a clue in the application, so if someone haven't seen the FAQ, they don't know.\n\nThis is a problem because Atom is then collecting data WITHOUT consent, even if it is in the FAQ and even if the user has downloaded the application.\n\nBesides, I find the whole concept of tracking users with the excuse of collecting useful data ridiculous!\n\nIn the entire history of Open Source this has never been needed and users are extremely helpful in sharing information, data, and reports about bugs, how they use the application, and other stuff.\n\nThe metrics package in Atom should to be removed from the default install, and then you can leave the package for anyone who want to install it by himself from the installation menu. Or as suggested, leave it OFF at first.\n\nAnother important point is that Atom is NOT simply collecting statistical data! If that where the case there certainly is no need to create a SHA1 of each installation MAC address. That is NOT collecting statistical data, that is specific and individual surveillance, which is unacceptable.\n","author":{"url":"https://github.com/greencopper","@type":"Person","name":"greencopper"},"datePublished":"2015-01-09T23:11:36Z","url":"https://github.com/atom/atom/issues/4966"}</script><div data-team-hovercards-enabled="true" class="markdown-body" data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">You need to leave the metrics disabled by default and then at least ask users, first time they activate the editor, whether they would allow it to be enabled.</p>
<p dir="auto">I for one will not allow spyware to run on my box, hence I disable or remove such applications, but Atom doesn't provide a clue in the application, so if someone haven't seen the FAQ, they don't know.</p>
<p dir="auto">This is a problem because Atom is then collecting data WITHOUT consent, even if it is in the FAQ and even if the user has downloaded the application.</p>
<p dir="auto">Besides, I find the whole concept of tracking users with the excuse of collecting useful data ridiculous!</p>
<p dir="auto">In the entire history of Open Source this has never been needed and users are extremely helpful in sharing information, data, and reports about bugs, how they use the application, and other stuff.</p>
<p dir="auto">The metrics package in Atom should to be removed from the default install, and then you can leave the package for anyone who want to install it by himself from the installation menu. Or as suggested, leave it OFF at first.</p>
<p dir="auto">Another important point is that Atom is NOT simply collecting statistical data! If that where the case there certainly is no need to create a SHA1 of each installation MAC address. That is NOT collecting statistical data, that is specific and individual surveillance, which is unacceptable.</p></div></div><div class="IssueBodyTaskList__-FlQre"><div role="toolbar" I don't give a shit about whether or not Github knows how I use Atom, my IP (which they may already get every time I log in to their website, don't know) or the color of underwear I am wearing while writing code.</p>
<p dir="auto">But I respect that most people are very much concerned about it. All I am saying is that, as long as people are made aware of this package existing (and what info it collects) when they first install or use the product, and are given the option to not be subject to that data collection, then it's become much much less of a real problem than overly excitable people want to keep believing it is.</p>
<p dir="auto">Let's level here... we're talking about intelligent people, mostly developers, arguably the most tech-aware type of human being that walks the earth!  And you're seriously telling me that these people either can't be trusted to (or are utterly unable) to read the introduction text on a welcome page and make up their own minds what to do about it? Gimme a break.</p>
<p dir="auto">This sanctimonious fake-outrage about something this minor is bordering on trolling in my eyes.</p>
<p dir="auto">Having said that, though... If it's true that the data collection - as it is being done by the metrics package right now (!) - is illegal in some places (and I am not convinced until someone can point out exactly which part of it makes it so), then it is best to remove it (since the alternative, an opt-in model, would render it completely useless as I mentioned earlier).<br>
Not because it's truly morally necessary (it isn't), but because it's common sense to not break the law.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 <ul dir="auto">
<li>I, and I believe everyone else here, respect people's choice to disable the metrics package or simply uninstall Atom altogether. Everyone has to make a decision as to how best to protect their own privacy.</li>

<ol dir="auto">
<li>
<p dir="auto">How is someone supposed to know about this "Metrics" package? I've been using Atom since January 2015 and I only knew about this matter a few days ago thanks to a friend of mine who tweeted about it.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p dir="auto">Disabling the package <strong>after</strong> is too late, because it will have already transmitted user data.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p dir="auto">I really hope this conversation remains constructive until the issue is resolved, and I hope Atom developers will be able to escalate the problem to the right department.</p>
<p dir="auto">I don't think anybody is here just to make noise or offend anyone. You are doing an amazing job with Atom and I thank you for this, but users privacy matters too and I would expect you to have respect for it.</p>

<p dir="auto">As I mentioned above, personally I don't care about the data that the metrics package collects, as it's really minor stuff [...]</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">This must have been gone over before.. but:</p>
<p dir="auto"><a href="https://github.com/atom/metrics#collected-data">https://github.com/atom/metrics#collected-data</a></p>
<blockquote>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>A unique UUID v4 random identifier is generated according to [RFC4122][RFC4122]</li>
<li>The screen width and height</li>
<li>The version of Atom being used</li>
<li>The name of each view class or atom configuration file opened in a pane, e.g. <code class="notranslate">EditorView</code>, <code class="notranslate">SettingsView</code>,<br>
<code class="notranslate">MarkdownPreviewView</code>, and <code class="notranslate">UserKeymap</code>. No other pane item information is collected.</li>
<li>Exception messages (without paths)</li>
<li>Commands run (save core commands)</li>
<li>The amount of time the current window was open for</li>
<li>The amount of time the current window took to load</li>
<li>The amount of time the app took to launch</li>
<li>The app's release channel (stable, beta, dev)</li>
<li>Deprecations: package name and version of each deprecation</li>
</ul>
</blockquote>
<hr>
<p dir="auto">That is.. extraordinarily minor. Atom has even taken the time to sanitize exception messages (by removing paths). <a href="http://www.infoworld.com/article/2979054/windows-security/windows-7-8-10-now-all-collecting-user-data-for-microsoft.html" rel="nofollow">Microsoft</a> collects more. Ubuntu collects more. <a href="https://www.google.com/analytics/" rel="nofollow">Almost</a> <a href="https://www.intercom.io/" rel="nofollow">every</a> <a href="http://get.gaug.es/" rel="nofollow">website</a> collects more.</p>
<p dir="auto">If it were me.. I'd collect a lot more:</p>
<ul dir="auto">
<li>Properties of each file opened: <code class="notranslate">file type</code>, <code class="notranslate">size</code>, <code class="notranslate">number of lines</code>, <code class="notranslate">longest line</code>, <code class="notranslate">time to open</code>, <code class="notranslate">time to save</code></li>
<li>A ping to track active usage and how long that looks like</li>
<li>Properties of each "ctrl-p" search result: <code class="notranslate">number of results</code>, <code class="notranslate">time to search</code>, <code class="notranslate">length of search term</code>, <code class="notranslate">position of file in list chosen</code></li>
<li>Properties of each "find" search result: <code class="notranslate">number of files in results</code>, <code class="notranslate">number of results</code>, <code class="notranslate">time to search</code>, <code class="notranslate">length of search term</code>, <code class="notranslate">number of results visited</code>.</li>
<li>Name and version of each package used (and if its disabled)</li>
<li>Number of windows opened</li>
<li>How long a window is open for before it is closed (more of active usage)</li>
<li>How long a window is idle for (more of active usage)</li>
</ul></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li href="https://github.com/batjko">@batjko</a> Well yes I can definitely see why people would choose to turn it on to help the core developers. Being opt-in is not at odds with because such users can just, opt-in. Basically my view is the ideal of nothing should be phoning home by default. Yes it's great that it's free (for whatever definition of free you mean, gratis or libre), but that still doesn't excuse it collecting usage info by default. As in, it doesn't make it 'perfect' for my 'ideals', and I want to it to be 'perfect', because why not? Or rather, what are the developers really missing out on if it becomes opt-in? If it's just these metrics, then really they should be, in my opinion, making it opt-in because they don't risk 'scaring off' users, and thus potential contributors. (Because you know, how are these metrics <em>really</em> useful to atom?)</p>
<p dir="auto">But I think the only way they can 'justify' keeping it opt-out is if Google is paying them a significant enough amount of money to keep it opt-out (because obviously google knows that making it opt-in will potentially make it useless as you say). Because that way if they make it opt-in, they lose <em>money</em>, meaning atom will have less manpower/developers working on it, potentially causing its development to deteriorate. (My personal opinion would be that that doesn't matter since it's free software anyway so the community can keep it going, but I can still understand justifying keeping it opt-out because of money.)</p>
<p dir="auto">But if you just don't agree with my ideal that nothing should be phoning home by default, then I guess we'll have to agree to disagree and leave it at that.</p>
<p dir="auto"><a class="user-mention notranslate" data-hovercard-type="user" data-hovercard-url="/users/mehcode/hovercard" data-octo-click="hovercard-link-click" data-octo-dimensions="link_type:self" href="https://github.com/mehcode">@mehcode</a></p>

<p dir="auto">That is.. extraordinarily minor. Atom has even taken the time to sanitize exception messages (by removing paths). Microsoft collects more. Ubuntu collects more. Almost every website collects more.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">I don't think this is right. Just because they do "wrong" (in my opinion) things <em>more</em>, doesn't excuse another entity from doing "wrong" things less...</p>
<p dir="auto">Okay, Microsoft collects more, great, but what about those who don't use Windows? Then that's a moot point for them. Same with Ubuntu. Yes basically every website engages in 'tracking', but really atom is the only <em>editor</em> I've heard that engages in tracking usage stats by default (so far). <blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Is there a difference between an editor and a website? Does it matter? This is a strange argument.</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Yes. Maybe this is getting blurred with in-browser editors these days, but disregarding that, there is a difference between websites tracking your website visits and editors reporting on what you're doing in the editor.</p>
<blockquote>
<p dir="auto">It's far different from stealing.. Are you missing any possessions afterwords?</p>
</blockquote>
<p dir="auto">Missing the point, it's not that getting usage stats <em>is</em> stealing, it's that it is a 'bad' thing to do (by default), and other people doing bad things does not excuse us from doing bad things as well. So say if there are groups of bad people who actively engage in killing the innocent, it doesn't give us an excuse to kill only a few innocent, saying "oh well, all these other groups do a lot <em>worse</em> than us, so it's not <em>that</em> bad!". But really the point should be that killing even one innocent person is bad, so it's still not okay to do it. Yes, obviously tracking usage statistics is not the same as murder, I'm not saying it is.</p>
<p dir="auto">So yes, to agree with this view, you have to agree that phoning home by default is a fundamentally 'bad' thing to do to others. Maybe getting paid a lot of money (by google) justifies this for atom, which I still may not agree with but at least I can understand where they're coming from. But I don't understand keeping it opt-out if that isn't the case, because it doesn't seem like usage statistics alone are all that useful (as in worth it to risk scaring off potential users, and thus contributors). Maybe I'm wrong about that though.</p></div></div><div role="toolbar" aria-label="Reactions" class="d-flex gap-1 flex-wrap"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></li><li data-turbolinks="false"><div class="markdown-body safe-html-box__Uwc6Al"><p dir="auto">There's little point in complaining it is not opt-in.<br>
There's some very acute assumption on both camp.<br>
Maybe designing a proper opt-in experience could help lower the resistance or at least see better what's ahead of us.</p>
<p dir="auto">Two things I see is there's no good place to put that opt-in, and the quality of statistics.  We should replace the complains with an effort to solve the problem of improving atom with real life knowledge while respecting privacy.</p>
<p dir="auto">For one, Squirrel team are against adding a GUI to select options, and that's probably for the better because check-box at install time really scream spyware toolbar. However we can have a <em>"Help us improve Atom"</em> notification with the opt-in check box. That notification can appears at first start and at a few key moments like on errors, install of new packages and updates. Notification would state it sends a bit of information from the past, that way may be able to rebuild the error.</p>
